lines.say: A carbonyl is a carbon double bonded to an oxygen. It's flat, at 120 degrees.
Oxygen pulls the electrons. Carbon is delta plus, oxygen delta minus.

draw.alt: Carbonyl group with delta plus carbon, a nucleophile attacking carbon

lines.say: So the carbon is an electrophile. Nucleophiles attack it.
Acid protonates the oxygen and makes the carbon even more electrophilic.
Aldehydes and ketones have only H or carbon on the C=O.
Acids and their derivatives carry chlorine, oxygen or nitrogen, which can leave.
Can it leave? Then substitute. If not, add.

draw.alt: Two branches: aldehydes and ketones go to addition, acyl compounds go to substitution

lines.say: Afterwards, ask: did the C=O stay, or disappear?
The nucleophile bonds to carbon. The pi electrons move onto oxygen.
Carbon becomes tetrahedral. This is the tetrahedral intermediate, an alkoxide.

draw.alt: Flat carbonyl becomes a tetrahedral alkoxide, then an alcohol after protonation

lines.say: Then the alkoxide picks up H plus to give an alcohol.
Sodium borohydride adds hydride. Aldehydes give primary alcohols, ketones secondary.
Grignards add carbon. Methanal gives primary, aldehydes secondary, ketones tertiary.
Aldehydes react faster. Ketones have two alkyl groups that push and crowd.
Acyl compounds react by addition, then elimination.
Add the nucleophile. Then C=O reforms and pushes out the leaving group.

draw.alt: Leaving group L is crossed out and replaced by the nucleophile; the C=O is kept

lines.say: It's not SN2. The tetrahedral intermediate really exists.
Clever Animals Eat Apples: chloride, anhydride, ester, amide.
Weak base, good leaver. Chloride leaves easily. NH two minus is terrible.
Nitrogen also donates its lone pair into C=O, so amides are stable.

frames.heading: Sliding down to esters and amides

lines.say: You can always slide down to a less reactive derivative.

draw.alt: Water slide from acid chloride at top down to amide at bottom

lines.say: Acid chloride plus ethanol gives an ester and HCl.
With ammonia you need two equivalents, because HCl grabs one.
Fischer esterification is reversible. Use excess alcohol or remove water.
Basic hydrolysis is not reversible. The carboxylate won't be attacked.
Esters with excess Grignard react twice, giving a tertiary alcohol.
Carboxylic acids have pKa around four to five. Alcohols are around 16.
The carboxylate's charge is shared over two oxygens.
A hydrogen on the alpha carbon is unusually acidic, pKa about 19 to 20.

draw.alt: Removing the alpha hydrogen gives an enolate with charge shared between carbon and oxygen

lines.say: Keto and enol forms are tautomers. The keto form wins for simple ketones.
Enolates attack at the alpha carbon, forming new C–C bonds.
Acyl substitution is not a one-step SN2.
Aldehydes and ketones never substitute. H and R can't leave.
Excess Grignard on an ester doesn't stop at the ketone.
The enolate charge is shared, with most on oxygen.
Can it leave? Substitute. If not, add.
Chloride, anhydride, ester, amide. Slide downhill only.
Grignards and cyanide add carbons. Hydride reductions don't.
For acidity, argue through the stability of the conjugate base.
